pr.title: Optimize rhythm evaluation by replacing curve
pr.description:
It's replacing slow Math.Sin with much faster Smoothstep (9x faster execution for this line).
https://www.desmos.com/calculator/ta2lhnu6ug

golden.note:
`reverseDeltaDifferenceRatio` and the later `fraction = Math.Max(prevDelta / currDelta, ...)` both divide by `Math.Min(prevDelta, currDelta)` / `currDelta` etc. If `StrainTime` can ever be 0 (or extremely close), this will produce `Infinity/NaN` and destabilise difficulty.

Also, `SmoothstepBellCurve()` is designed around `x` in ~[0,1] (mean=0.5,width=0.5). The fractional-part calculation `x - (long)x` can lose precision for large ratios and doesn’t clamp against small floating overshoots (<0 or >1). Prefer `Math.Floor` and clamp to [0,1] before passing into `SmoothstepBellCurve`.

Suggested:
- Guard: `if (prevDelta <= 0 || currDelta <= 0) return 1.0;` (or skip bonus) consistent with intended behaviour.
- `var frac = reverse - Math.Floor(reverse); frac = Math.Clamp(frac, 0, 1);`
Comment for reverseDeltaDifferenceRatio inaccurately states value is in [0,1] (it is always ≥1); update to explain fractional part extraction for detecting delta multiples.
Fractional part calculation uses unsafe cast to long; replace with Math.Truncate to prevent overflow for large ratio values.

Doc/typo: summary says "returns returns" and "reducing it's value" -> "reducing its value". Also clarify expected output range: with current code, values outside [mean-width, mean+width] result in x<0 passed to Smoothstep; if Smoothstep clamps internally, fine. If not, output may go below 0. Consider explicitly clamping x to [0,width] before Smoothstep or mention reliance on Smoothstep clamping.
Documentation contains redundant word 'returns'. Should be 'Calculates a Smoothstep Bellcurve that returns 1 for x = mean, and smoothly reducing its value to 0 over width.'
Consider using more descriptive variable names to improve readability. Reusing 'x' for different purposes makes the logic harder to follow.
The ternary expression can be simplified to `Math.Abs(x)` for better readability. Both branches compute `width - Math.Abs(x)`, just written differently.
